title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
shortDefinition: A neural network architecture that routes each input to specialized sub-networks, improving efficiency at scale.
definition: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a neural network architecture where, instead of every input passing through the entire network, a 'routing' mechanism directs each input to only a relevant subset of specialized sub-networks ('experts') — allowing the overall model to have a very large total parameter count while only activating a fraction of those parameters for any given input, improving computational efficiency relative to an equivalently large 'dense' model that activates all parameters for every input. Several leading modern LLMs use MoE architecture to achieve strong capability with more efficient inference cost than a fully dense model of comparable total size.

sections.title: How mixture of experts improves efficiency
sections.description: MoE activates only a fraction of parameters per input, reducing inference cost while maintaining large total capacity.

content.text: In a dense neural network, every parameter is involved in processing every input, meaning inference cost scales directly with total model size. In an MoE architecture, a routing mechanism learns which specialized 'expert' sub-networks are most relevant for a given input and activates only those, leaving the rest of the model's parameters unused for that specific input. This means an MoE model can have a very large total parameter count (and the broad capability that implies) while keeping the actual compute cost per inference call closer to that of a much smaller dense model, since only a fraction of parameters are active at once.

items: Dense model — all parameters active for every input.
MoE model — routing activates only relevant experts.
Total parameters — MoE can be very large without per-inference cost scaling.
Compute efficiency — active parameters per input are much smaller.
Capability vs. cost — favorable tradeoff for large-scale models.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: MoE decouples total model size from per-inference compute cost — models can be huge in total parameters while keeping inference cost closer to that of a much smaller model.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of mixture of experts

content.text: MoE architecture has limitations. Routing mechanisms can introduce training instability or inconsistent output quality. The architecture is complex to implement and train, requiring significant engineering sophistication. Some research suggests potential tradeoffs in reasoning consistency compared to dense models, and memory requirements can still be high for serving multiple experts. MoE models may not outperform dense models for smaller-scale applications, and the cost-efficiency benefits are most pronounced at very large scales.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about mixture of experts

items.question: Do I need to know whether a model uses MoE architecture to use it effectively?
items.answer: No — this is a technical implementation detail handled by the model provider; ClickMasters considers it as one factor in model selection but it doesn't require business-stakeholder-level understanding.

items.question: Are MoE models always cheaper to use than dense models?
items.answer: Not necessarily in every case, but MoE architecture is specifically designed to improve the cost-efficiency tradeoff at large model scale, which can translate to favorable per-token pricing for some MoE-based provider offerings.

items.question: Which major LLM providers use MoE architecture?
items.answer: This varies and changes as providers update their models; ClickMasters tracks current provider architecture details and recommends accordingly during model selection.

items.question: Can MoE models have any downsides compared to dense models?
items.answer: Some research suggests potential tradeoffs in certain reasoning consistency scenarios, though this is an active area of ongoing development; ClickMasters validates actual performance against your specific use case rather than relying on architectural theory alone.

items.question: Will understanding MoE help me negotiate better pricing with AI providers?
items.answer: Indirectly — understanding why certain models offer different cost-per-capability ratios can inform smarter provider and model selection, which ClickMasters handles as part of project scoping.

items.question: What is the difference between MoE and ensemble models?
items.answer: MoE uses a routing mechanism to select a subset of experts for each input during inference. Ensembles run multiple complete models and combine their outputs. MoE is more computationally efficient because only a subset of parameters is activated per input.

items.question: What is the role of the router in MoE architecture?
items.answer: The router (or gating network) learns which expert sub-network is most relevant for a given input. It assigns weights to experts, typically activating only the top-k experts for each input to balance performance and efficiency.

items.question: Can MoE be combined with transformer architecture?
items.answer: Yes — many modern MoE implementations replace the feed-forward layers in transformers with MoE layers, while keeping the attention mechanisms dense. This combines the benefits of both architectures.

items.question: What is the difference between dense and sparse models?
items.answer: Dense models activate all parameters for every input. Sparse models (like MoE) activate only a subset of parameters per input. Sparse models can be much larger in total size while maintaining efficient inference.
